target: मेरी बहन डॉक्टर है।
english: My sister is a doctor.
tip: Hindi puts is/are at the very end: है (hai) or हैं (hain). मेरी बहन डॉक्टर है (meri bahan doctor hai) – literally 'my sister doctor is'.

target: नमस्ते, मेरा नाम अमित है।
english: Hello, my name is Amit.
tip: है / हैं / हूँ / हो (hai / hain / hun / ho) normally sit at the end of the sentence. Not in the middle like English is/are.

target: नमस्ते, कैसे हो तुम सब?
english: Hello, how are you all?
tip: Question words sit in the answer's slot: in कैसे हो (kaise ho = how are you), कैसे (kaise) fills the spot the answer ठीक (theek = fine) would take – no flipping to the front like English.

target: नमस्ते अंकल, आंटी कहाँ हैं?
english: Namaste uncle, where is aunty?
tip: Never drop है/हैं/हूँ. मैं डॉक्टर is not a sentence – you need मैं डॉक्टर हूँ (main doctor hun = I am a doctor).

target: अनीता, तुम्हारे बच्चे कैसे हैं?
english: Anita, how are your children?
tip: Possessives match the thing owned, not the owner: तुम्हारे बच्चे (tumhare bachche = your children) – तुम्हारे (tumhare) is plural because बच्चे is, whoever you are.

target: मुझे ज़ोरों की भूख लगी है।
english: I'm very hungry.
tip: Hunger strikes you in Hindi: भूख लगी है (bhookh lagi hai = hunger has struck). Thirst and cold too: प्यास लगी है (pyaas lagi hai). You're the target, not the doer.

target: मैं रोज़ सुबह दूध पीता हूँ।
english: I drink milk every morning.
tip: The verb ending shows the speaker's own gender: a man says पीता हूँ (peeta hun = I drink), a woman says पीती हूँ (peeti hun). Same I, different ending.

target: मेरे चाचाजी दिल्ली में रहते हैं।
english: My uncle lives in Delhi.
tip: जी (ji) glued to a name or relative adds respect: चाचाजी (chachaji = uncle-ji). You'll hear it everywhere – पापाजी (papaji), even हाँ जी (haan ji) for a polite yes.

target: मेरी माँ हर सुबह चाय बनाती है।
english: My mom makes tea every morning.
tip: Present habit ends -ता/-ती/-ते by gender: माँ बनाती है (maa banaati hai = mom makes-f).

target: क्या आप मुझे रास्ता बता सकते हैं?
english: Can you tell me the way?
tip: For polite आप or plural, use -ते: आप क्या करते हैं? (aap kya karte hain = What do you do?). Plural ending also signals respect.

target: बच्चों को चॉकलेट केक बहुत पसंद आया।
english: The children really liked the chocolate cake.
tip: पसंद आया (pasand aaya = liking came) is one-time – they liked it that day. For a standing taste, Hindi switches to पसंद है (pasand hai).

target: शहद चीनी से ज़्यादा सेहतमंद होता है।
english: Honey is healthier than sugar.
tip: No word for 'than' – Hindi uses से (se = from): चीनी से ज़्यादा (chini se zyada = from sugar more) means 'more than sugar'.

target: मेरे पोते-पोतियाँ मुझसे बहुत प्यार करते हैं।
english: My grandchildren love me very much.
tip: Love is something you do in Hindi: प्यार करते हैं (pyaar karte hain = do love). And the loved one takes से: मुझसे (mujhse = literally 'from me').

target: विजय हर रोज़ नहाकर तैयार होता है।
english: Vijay bathes and gets ready every day.
tip: Hindi chains actions with -कर (-kar = having done): नहाकर (nahakar = having bathed) means 'after bathing' – no 'and' needed between bathing and getting ready.

target: बस अड्डे तक पैदल कितना समय लगता है?
english: How much time does it take to walk to the bus stand?
tip: English 'takes time' flips in Hindi: समय लगता है (samay lagta hai = time attaches). The time attaches to the task – the task doesn't take it.

target: अगर मौसम ठीक रहा तो हम मुंबई चलेंगे।
english: If the weather stays fine, we will go to Mumbai.
tip: English drops 'then' but Hindi keeps it: अगर (agar = if) pairs with तो (to = then). Skipping the तो sounds unfinished to Hindi ears.

target: रमेश रोज़ सुबह दौड़ता है।
english: Ramesh runs every morning.
tip: दौड़ता है (daudta hai) = runs, as a routine – not 'is running'. Right-now actions use रहा है (raha hai); the -ता (-ta) form is for habits.

target: मैं रोज़ सुबह दाँत साफ़ करता हूँ।
english: I brush my teeth every morning.
tip: There's no verb 'brush' here – Hindi makes teeth clean: दाँत साफ़ करता हूँ (daant saaf karta hoon). साफ़ (saaf = clean) + करना (karna = do) does the job.

target: वह हमेशा सच बोलता है।
english: He always speaks the truth.
tip: English 'tells' the truth – Hindi speaks it: सच बोलता है (sach bolta hai). Truth and lies both pair with बोलना (bolna = speak), and there's no 'the'.

target: ये गाड़ियाँ बहुत तेज़ चलती हैं।
english: These cars run very fast.
tip: ये गाड़ियाँ चलती हैं (chalti hain) – literally 'walk'. चलना (chalna) is the verb for machines moving or working: cars, phones and fans all चलते (chalte).

target: मैं रोज़ सुबह-सुबह अख़बार पढ़ता हूँ।
english: I read the newspaper every morning.
tip: Doubling a word tightens its meaning: सुबह (subah) = morning, सुबह-सुबह (subah-subah) = early in the morning, right at daybreak.

target: दादी हर शाम मंदिर जाती हैं।
english: Grandmother goes to the temple every evening.
tip: One grandmother, plural verb: दादी जाती हैं (daadi jaati hain), not है (hai). Elders take plural forms as respect – singular would sound rude.

target: सुनीता बहुत मेहनत से पढ़ाई करती है।
english: Sunita studies very hard.
tip: 'Studies' is noun + do: पढ़ाई करती है (padhaai karti hai = does studying). Hindi builds many verbs this way – काम करना (kaam karna = to work).

target: बच्चे स्कूल से आकर होमवर्क करते हैं।
english: Children do homework after coming from school.
tip: -कर (-kar) chains actions: स्कूल से आकर (school se aakar = having come from school). One small ending replaces the whole phrase 'after coming'.

target: वह हमेशा समय पर काम पर पहुँचता है।
english: He always reaches work on time.
tip: You arrive 'on' work: काम पर (kaam par) पहुँचता है. पर is literally 'on', but it's the standard word for being at or heading to work.

target: क्या तुम्हारी बहन भी तुम्हारे साथ रहती है?
english: Does your sister also live with you?
tip: भी (bhi = also) sits right after the word it highlights: तुम्हारी बहन भी (tumhaari bahan bhi) = your sister too. Move भी and the emphasis moves with it.

target: वह दिन-रात बहुत मेहनत से पढ़ाई करता है।
english: He studies very hard day and night.
tip: Hindi pairs opposites with a hyphen and skips 'and': दिन-रात (din-raat = day and night). Same pattern in माता-पिता (maata-pita = parents).

target: मेरी पत्नी अदरक वाली बहुत अच्छी चाय बनाती है।
english: My wife makes very good ginger tea.
tip: वाली (vaali) tags what something comes with: अदरक वाली चाय (adrak vaali chai) = ginger tea, roughly 'the ginger one'. Masculine nouns take वाला (vaala).

target: मैं यह दवा दिन में दो बार लेता हूँ।
english: I take this medicine twice a day.
tip: 'Twice a day' is 'in a day two times': दिन में दो बार (din mein do baar). Everyday Hindi skips 'per' – में (mein = in) plus the time span covers it.

target: यह दुकान रात नौ बजे बंद होती है।
english: This shop closes at nine at night.
tip: English shops just 'close' – Hindi shops become closed: बंद होती है (band hoti hai = gets closed). A person closing it would be बंद करना (band karna).
